Each test is mechanical enough that two reviewers reach the same verdict. Where a test needs judgement, it says what evidence settles it.
| Name the day the project finishes. If no answer exists in principle, not merely today | It is not a project. It is an area, a view, or ongoing work |
| Would you open one pull request for this issue? If it needs several by different people | It is a parent, or it is a project |
| Would each sub-issue make sense in a list without its parent's title? If not | It is a checklist wearing sub-issues |
| Can a filter produce the membership of this initiative? If yes, and no tradeoffs are made across its projects | It is a view |
| Does the issue describe a code change with no stated consequence outside the codebase? | It belongs in a pull request |
| Read the title alone, with no properties visible. Can you say what will be different when it is done? | Vague |
| Does the title contain a type, priority, status, team, component tag, or date? | Restates a property |
| Does it contain "and", or two verbs with different objects? | Two objects |
| Is it a bare noun or noun phrase for an issue or project? | A topic, not a change |
| Is it an outcome-shaped object named after a mechanism that might not achieve the outcome? | Mechanism title. Correct only when delivering the mechanism is the point |
| Does a bug title assert a cause or a fix? | Presumes the diagnosis |
| Does the description contradict a later comment, a status, or the current code? | Stale |
| Is an open question listed that has since been answered anywhere? | Answered, still listed |
| Do acceptance criteria refer to scope that was dropped? | Stale criteria |
| Does the description contain "we assume", "for now", or "to be confirmed" written more than a month ago? | Unverified assumption, ageing |
| Is the project description describing where the work stands? | Status in the wrong place |
| Would this line be false after the pull request merges? | Belongs in the pull request |
| Does the object contain SQL, a full stack trace, test code, or a migration script? | Route out. Keep only the existence, risk, and reversibility |
| Does it name a file or symbol, and is the issue not delegated to an agent and not about that file as a deliverable? | Route out |
| Is a decision that is expensive to reverse recorded only in a comment? | Needs an ADR, using `writing-adrs` |
| Does a comment thread contain the reasoning for the current shape of the system? | Promote a decision note, and write an ADR if architectural |
| Is a paragraph of investigation notes in a description rather than a comment? | Wrong place, even though the content is fine |
| Does any heading hold less than a paragraph? | Empty heading |
| Does the first sentence restate the title? | Wasted first sentence |
| Are there headings on an object under about 150 words? | Structure without content |
| Do `Context`, `Overview`, `Summary`, or `Next steps` appear with nothing under them that the rest does not already say? | Template residue |
| Is the same fact stated in the summary, the description, and the latest update? | Duplication. Keep it in the one place its reader looks |
| Is the project summary empty, a fragment, or describing a different project? | Broken summary, the most-read field in the workspace |
| Name the saved view or automation that consumes this label | If you cannot, delete or archive it |
| How many open issues carry it, and when was it last applied? | Unused |
| Does another label mean the same thing, in different words or casing? | Duplicate, merge |
| Does it restate a property? | Delete |
| Do several labels share a prefix without being a group? | Mutual exclusivity is unenforced. Consider a group, but only after the set is small |
| Does it have a description? | Undescribed labels are applied by guesswork |
| Can the name be true? Read it as a sentence: "X is now true" | If not, it is a phase label |
| Does it name a team, a discipline, or a layer? | Not an outcome |
| Is it numbered rather than named? | Carries no information |
| Does its progress bar mean anything to someone outside the team? | If not, it is internal bookkeeping |
| Remove every sentence derivable from the issue list and the project description. Is anything left? | Manufactured update |
| Does it state percentages or issue counts? | Duplicates the generated progress report |
| Does the health value match the rule in `writing-linear-updates`? | Health by feel |
| Is a blocker described, with health `onTrack`? | Contradiction |
| Is the target date unaddressed while the update reports a slip? | Missing the sentence readers need |
| When was the last update, and does the project have a schedule? | Overdue, though Linear flags this itself |

description: Creates or restructures work in Linear, the issue tracker. Covers issues, projects, milestones, initiatives, sub-issues, comments, documents, and the words that link a Linear issue from a pull request or merge request so merging completes it, and decides whether something belongs in Linear at all, or in a repository issue, a pull request, or an ADR. Use when asked to file, plan, split, rewrite, or move a specific piece of work. For a bulk audit of existing Linear content, use reviewing-linear instead. Not for GitHub or GitLab issues, which writing-repository-issues owns.

Work gets filed as whatever object is nearest, with detail invented to fill a template, and then rewritten later by an agent that had not read what was already there. This skill exists to stop those three things.
The conventions live in `linear-conventions`. Invoke that skill if it is not already loaded, and read the one reference file that answers the question in front of you rather than all of them.
## Three modes, and which one you are in
| Mode | What you produce | Authorised by |
| Draft | Text in the conversation. Nothing touches Linear | Any request to write, plan, or rephrase something |
| Propose | A preview of the exact object, its properties, and its body, with unknowns listed | The default when someone asks for work to be filed |
| Write | A call to the Linear MCP server | An explicit yes to the preview, or an instruction that plainly authorises writing |

Default to propose. Never move to write because the draft came out well, because an existing object could be phrased better, or because the change looks obviously right. A better version is not authorisation.

An instruction such as "create an issue for this" authorises creation, and still gets a preview first, because the preview is where the wrong project, the invented date, or the missing unknown gets caught. An instruction such as "just create it, no preview" removes the preview and nothing else.
Spend the reads. Almost every bad object comes from writing before looking.
1. **The request**, for what is actually being asked.
2. **The repository**, for what is true. The state of the code decides scope more often than the request does.
3. **Existing Linear objects.** Look for an issue or project that already covers this. If one exists, return it and say whether it covers the request, rather than creating a near-duplicate.
4. **The target team's statuses and labels**, so you use what exists rather than inventing vocabulary.
5. **Existing ADRs**, in `docs/adr/`, when the work could touch an architectural decision.

The Linear MCP server is configured as `linear-server`, and its tools appear as `mcp__linear-server__*`. If it is unavailable, produce the object as markdown for someone to paste, and say that is what you did.
`.agents/skills/linear-conventions/references/objects.md` holds the decision framework. The short form:
- One reviewable outcome with one owner is an **issue**.
- An outcome with a definable end, spanning enough issues to need coordination, is a **project**.
- Two or more projects sharing an outcome, with real tradeoffs between them, is an **initiative**.
- A state a project passes through that a stakeholder would notice is a **milestone**.
- A recurring question with a computable answer is a **view**, not an object.
- Something with no end state is not a project, whatever it is called.

If the work turns out to be technical execution detail rather than an outcome, route it. `.agents/skills/linear-conventions/references/boundary.md` decides between a repository issue, the pull request, and an ADR. Say where you routed it and why, rather than filing it in Linear anyway.

If the work is too large for one issue, propose a parent and a small set of children. The same holds for any structure you would create in one go, such as a project with milestones or an initiative with projects: show the whole shape first, and create none of it until it is approved.
### Sometimes the answer is no object

Filing work nobody will read costs more than it saves. Recommend creating nothing when the change is small, self-contained, and has no consequence anyone would ask about later: renaming an internal key and its call sites, a dependency bump, a lint fix, a comment correction. The pull request is the record, and it is a better one, because it shows the change.
Say so plainly, with the reason, and offer the pull request as the alternative. If the user wants it tracked anyway, track it. This is advice, not a veto.

Titles follow `.agents/skills/linear-conventions/references/naming.md`. Bodies follow `.agents/skills/linear-conventions/references/writing.md`. Shapes for the common kinds of work are in `references/archetypes.md`, and they are patterns to draw from, not templates to fill.
Choose the least structure that improves comprehension. For most issues that is a title and one or two sentences.
Set only the properties you were given or can read from the system. Leave the rest empty. An empty property is a legible unknown; a guessed one is a fact nobody chose.
1. **Read the current state**, including comments and linked objects, before proposing a single change.
2. **Understand why it says what it says.** A sentence that reads oddly is often the one fact someone needed.
3. **Preserve every useful fact.** Anything you cannot show to be obsolete stays.

4. **Relocate rather than delete.** Implementation detail moves to the pull request or a repository issue, evidence moves to a comment, decisions move to an ADR. Say in your response what moved where.
5. **Do not rewrite for style alone.** Rewriting is justified by information that is wrong, missing, stale, or in the wrong place. "I would have phrased it differently" is not a justification.

**Leaving it alone is a result.** When an object is accurate, current, and readable, say so and change nothing. A rewriting skill that always rewrites is worse than no skill: it burns attention, churns history, and teaches people to stop reading the diffs.

When you remove a superseded requirement, keep the one line that explains why the direction changed, if that reason still shapes the current scope. Delete the dead requirement, not the reason it died.

Prefer patch operations over resending a whole description. The Linear MCP tools accept a list of edits anchored on exact text, applied atomically, which keeps the parts you did not touch exactly as they were. Send a full description only when you are genuinely replacing all of it.

When an assumption has been invalidated, remove it from the description and leave a comment saying what changed and when. Do not leave contradictory text in place for the sake of history: Linear keeps the history, and the description is the only thing anyone reads.
## Linking a Linear issue to a pull request

On GitHub, Linear links through the branch name, the pull request title or body, or a commit message; on GitLab, through the branch name, the merge request title or its description, never a comment or commit message. **The verb decides what happens on merge**, because Linear's pull request automations are configured per team and the documented defaults move the issue to In Progress when a pull request opens and to Done when it merges.
| Merging contributes to it | `ref`, `refs`, `references`, `part of`, `contributes to`, `toward`, `towards` |
| Do not link at all | `skip` or `ignore` before the identifier |

GitHub: the words above, from Linear's GitHub documentation; GitLab: Linear documents the same closing words, adds `updates` to the contributing ones, counts `related to` as contributing, and does not document `refs`, `toward`, `relates to`, `skip` or `ignore`.

Use a closing word only when merging genuinely finishes the work. **Check the team's configured automations and its workflow states before assuming**: a team whose states stop at Done has nowhere to move afterwards, so a closing word there makes merge equal completion. A team with a Released or Deployed state can afford one earlier.
The full list, with the reasoning, is in `references/accuracy.md`. Read it before your first write in a session.

Never invent an owner, a date, a status, a priority, a metric, a customer's demand, a decision, a dependency, a blocker, or the fact that something is finished. If a value would be a guess, leave it unset and say so in the preview.

Distinguish what you know from what you worked out. Mark facts read from a system, statements made by a person, and inferences you drew, and never let an inference become a fact because it made the sentence read better.
- Object type, title, and target team or project
- Properties you intend to set, and the ones you are deliberately leaving empty
- The full body as it will appear
- Unknowns, each with what would resolve it
- Anything you are routing out of Linear, and where to
- For an edit, what changes, what you are removing, and where it goes instead
Keep it scannable. The preview is the last point where a wrong project or an invented date is cheap to fix.
- The object type is the one the framework chose, not the one that was easiest.
- The title stands alone in a notification, and repeats no property.
- The first sentence says what changes and for whom, without restating the title.
- No heading holds less than a paragraph, and no section was added by habit.
- Nothing in the body would be false once the pull request merges.
- Every date, number, and name came from a system or a person.
- Unknowns are stated rather than filled.
- Nothing was written to Linear without approval.

"prompt": "File a GitLab issue for the flaky checkout test.",

An invented fact in a tracker is indistinguishable from a real one within a week, and it will be acted on. This is the one area where being unhelpful is cheaper than being wrong.
- Unknown is not the same as not applicable
Every statement is one of these, and the writing should make clear which.
| Known | Read from a system, or stated by a person | Plain assertion: "The API returns 400 for accounts with two providers." |
| Inferred | Worked out from evidence, and the evidence is shown | "The two failing tenants both have two providers configured, so the trigger is probably the ambiguous binding." |
| Proposed | A recommendation awaiting a decision | "Proposed: drop private replies from the first release." |
| Unknown | Not established | "Unknown: whether teams need private replies. Nobody has asked." |

Never promote a statement up this table to make a sentence read better. An inference written as a fact is the most common way a tracker becomes untrustworthy, because the evidence that would let a reader check it is gone.
| Owner or lead | Never assign. Leave unassigned and say it is unassigned |
| Status | Never move an object to a status that asserts work you did not observe. Finding a merged pull request is observation. Assuming one exists is not |
| Priority | Never set or change it. Priority is a human tradeoff between things you cannot see |

| Dates | Only a date that exists in a system or was stated by a person. Never estimate a completion date. When a date is needed but unknown, use a coarser resolution such as a quarter rather than inventing a day |
| Scope | Never silently widen or narrow. Propose scope changes and let someone accept them |
| Metrics | Every number carries its source and the date it was measured. No number without a measurement |
| Customer or user impact | Only from a customer request, a quoted message, or a stated fact. Never inferred from the nature of the bug. "Users are frustrated" is invention unless a user said so |
| Decisions | Only record a decision you can attribute to a person and a date. Your own recommendation is labelled as a recommendation |
| Dependencies | Only create a relation when the ordering is real. Two things concerning the same area are not related in the Linear sense |
| Blockers | A blocker is something that stops work, named specifically. "Might be blocked by the schema work" is not a blocker, it is a risk |
| Completion | Never claim work is done from a plan, a branch name, or a draft pull request |
## Unknown is not the same as not applicable
Leaving something out because it does not apply is correct, and silent. A bug affecting one tenant needs no scope section, and its absence says nothing.

Stating an unknown is for a gap that matters: something a reader would otherwise assume you had established. "Unknown: whether this reproduces in staging" earns its line. "Unknown: the marketing implications" does not.

When you cannot tell which one you are looking at, ask whether a reader would act differently knowing the answer. If not, leave it out rather than listing it as unknown. A wall of unknowns reads as diligence and works as noise.
A number someone states is evidence about their belief, not a measurement. Keep it, and keep its status with it.
> Affects roughly 30% of users. Estimate from Dana on 2026-08-13, not measured.

Do not round it into authority by writing "affects 30% of users", and do not drop it because it is soft. That estimate is often the only reason anyone prioritised the work, so losing it loses the argument.
"A customer asked for X" and "we are building X" are different facts, and collapsing them is how a roadmap acquires commitments nobody made.

Record a request as a request, attributed: a Linear customer request where that feature is in use, otherwise the customer's own words quoted in the issue. Record a decision only when a person made it, with who and when. An issue sitting in the backlog is not a commitment, and its description should not read like one.
An unknown is not an apology and does not need a paragraph. It needs the gap and what closes it.
> Unknown: whether the search index change is a day or a week. The spike on 2026-08-18 settles it.

Two failure modes to avoid. Do not hedge everything, because a document where every sentence is uncertain carries no information. Do not bury the unknown at the bottom, because the person who could resolve it is scanning.

When the request itself cannot be answered without information you do not have, say what is missing and stop. Do not produce a plausible object and hope. One good question beats a confident draft that has to be unpicked later.
Rewriting destroys more information than it creates unless the rewrite is disciplined.
Read the whole object first, including comments and linked issues. Then classify every sentence as: still true and useful, still true but belongs elsewhere, no longer true, or you cannot tell.

Keep the first. Relocate the second and say where it went. Remove the third and leave a comment recording what changed, if anyone might have relied on it. **Keep anything in the fourth category.** An oddly specific sentence you do not understand is usually the one fact someone needed and nobody else recorded.
Prefer patch operations anchored on exact text over resending the whole body, so the parts you did not consider stay exactly as they were.
In your response, list what you removed and where each piece went. A rewrite whose losses are invisible cannot be reviewed, and one that cannot be reviewed will eventually be reverted wholesale.

Patterns, not templates. Take the parts that carry information for this specific object and leave the rest. Worked before-and-after pairs are in `.agents/skills/linear-conventions/references/examples.md`.
| Small change | Title, then one or two sentences saying what is wrong and what will be true instead | Everything else |
| Bug | Observed, expected, where and when it was seen, one line of evidence in a collapsible | Cause, fix, and priority language |

| Feature or engineering change | Outcome sentence, why now with its evidence, then only what would surprise someone: non-goals, or how we will know it works | Restated context, acceptance criteria that repeat the title |
| Delegated to an agent | Outcome sentence, where to start, the existing pattern to reuse, and what must not change | Product background the agent cannot act on |
| Spike | The question as a question, the decision it unblocks, a timebox, and what it produces | Speculation about the answer |
| Chore or operational task | One sentence, and the trigger if it is recurring | A justification nobody asked for |

Take only the parts that carry information. When the expected behaviour is obvious from the observed one, stating it is ceremony: "clicking Retry sometimes submits the payment twice" does not need "expected: one payment". When you do not know where it was seen, say that in the same sentence rather than leaving a heading with nothing under it.
A bug title is declarative. Every other issue title is imperative.
Use a parent when one outcome has to split across people, teams, or pull requests. Not for a checklist you will work through yourself.

The parent carries the outcome and the context. Each child carries its own slice and reads sensibly in a list without its parent's title. Children inherit team, priority, and project from the parent, but not labels, so set labels explicitly if they matter.
Propose the split before creating it. A tree created without approval is tedious to undo.
What belongs in the summary and the description is in `.agents/skills/linear-conventions/references/writing.md`. This is the order that avoids rework:
1. **The description**, so you find out what the project actually is.
2. **The summary**, written last, once you know.
3. **Dates at honest resolution.** Linear accepts a year, half, quarter, month, or day, so use the coarsest one that is true rather than a precise date nobody believes.
4. **A lead**, only if someone has actually taken it.
The decision here is whether any should exist. Create them only when the project passes through states a stakeholder would notice, which a project of three issues does not.
A target date on a milestone is optional, and a wrong one is worse than none.
Only when two or more projects share an outcome and someone makes tradeoffs between them. One project is a project. A filterable grouping is a view.
Two to four short paragraphs: what changes at the company level, why now, what it will not do, how we will know it worked. The projects underneath are visible, so do not list them.
A document is justified when depth outlives an issue and more than one issue would link to it: a specification, a research write-up, a contract under design, a runbook.
It is not the place for a decision, which is an ADR, or for code detail, which is the repository. If you cannot name who opens it and why, do not create it.

description: Writes Linear project and initiative updates that report what changed since the last one, choose a health value by rule, and say what it means for the target date. Use when asked for a project update, an initiative update, a status update, or a summary of where a project stands.
An update answers one question: what changed since the last one, and what does it mean?
It is not a summary of the project. The project already describes itself, and anyone reading the update can see it. Restating it is the most common way an update ends up saying nothing.

Linear attaches a generated progress report to updates, covering overall progress, milestone movement, target date changes, and lead changes, and it only appears when progress moved by more than a couple of percent. So the numbers are already there. What the writing must add is judgement: why it moved, what it means for the date, and what someone should do about it.
- **The previous update**, and its date. Everything in this update is a delta from that point.
- **Issues that changed status since then**, and milestone progress.
- **Target date and scope changes** since then.
- **Open blockers**, including `blocked by` relations and project dependencies.
- **Anything the user told you**, which outranks all of it, because they know things the workspace does not.
If there is no previous update, this one covers the period since the project started, and says so in three words.
Health is `onTrack`, `atRisk`, or `offTrack`. Set it as the property. Do not also write it in prose beyond the opening word.
| `onTrack` | Target date and scope are unchanged, and no blocker is more than a week old |
| `atRisk` | A blocker exists with no owner or no date, or the date holds only if something uncertain goes right |
| `offTrack` | The date or the scope will change, and this update is where that is said |

Choosing by rule rather than by feel is what makes health comparable across projects and over time. If you cannot tell which value applies, say what you would need to know and propose the more pessimistic one.
Five to eight lines. No headings at that length.
3. **What it means** for the target date or scope. This is the sentence readers actually need.
4. **What is blocked or uncertain**, and who can unblock it.
5. **The next meaningful event**, with a date if one exists.
Leave out any of 2 to 5 that has nothing in it. Do not write a heading for an empty one.
- A restatement of the project description
- Percentages or issue counts, which Linear attaches on its own
- A list of completed issues, which the issue list already shows
- "Continuing to make progress", "working hard", and their relatives
- An invented cause for a slip
Post nothing, or post two lines. Both are correct, and which one depends on whether anyone is waiting.

Post nothing when the project is simply moving slowly and nothing is blocked. Linear flags projects that are overdue for an update on its own, so silence is already reported, and it is a more honest signal than a manufactured one.
Post two lines when something is stuck: name the blocker, say how long it has been there, and say who can clear it. Health is `atRisk` or `offTrack`, never `onTrack`.
Never manufacture progress. An update saying "work continues" turns a true unknown into a false healthy signal, which is worse than the silence it replaced.

An initiative update carries cross-project judgement only: a reallocation, a change of sequence, a bet that changed. If it could be reconstructed by concatenating the project updates underneath it, do not post it.

Draft, show the draft, and post only after approval. Include with the draft the facts it rests on and the proposed health value, so both can be checked before anything is published. Posting to Linear also posts to any connected Slack channel, so it is not a private act.

If nothing in the workspace supports a claim you want to make, do not make it. Accuracy rules are in `.agents/skills/tracking-work-in-linear/references/accuracy.md`, and they apply here without exception.
- It says what changed, not what the project is.
- The health value follows the rule, and the rule is defensible from the facts listed.
- The target date is either confirmed or explicitly moved.
- No percentages, no issue counts, no activity log.
- Nothing is claimed that the workspace or the user did not establish.
- If nothing changed, it says so in two lines or does not exist.

This case fails if health is onTrack despite the unscoped blocker, the target date goes unaddressed, a percentage or count appears, or a date stays relative.",

description: Writes and reviews the documentation in Terraform code to one fixed standard, covering the labelled Purpose, Rationale, Security, Caution and See header above every resource, data source and module call, the comments owed on lifecycle rules, depends_on, count, for_each and security settings, variable and output descriptions, locals, and module READMEs whose reference terraform-docs generates, with a checker for every rule a script can decide. Use when adding or changing .tf files, documenting or reviewing a Terraform module or root configuration, writing a variable or output description, setting up terraform-docs or TFLint documentation rules, or making Terraform or OpenTofu documentation consistent, including requests that say IaC or HCL without naming Terraform. For a repository's landing README with no .tf files beside it use writing-repository-readmes, and for architecture decision records use writing-adrs.

Terraform code has two readers, and each looks in one place. A **maintainer** edits the code: they read HCL fluently and need to know why it is the way it is. A **consumer** calls the module or runs the configuration: they read the `description` strings and the README, and never open `main.tf`. Every fact goes where its reader looks, once, in the same shape everywhere, so that a person, `grep` and the checker can all rely on it.
**Consistency outranks style.** Where this skill fixes a format, use it exactly, even where another phrasing would read better.
1. **Why, never what.** A comment that restates the block type, a name, an argument or a value is deleted, not reworded.

2. **One fact, one place, at the narrowest scope that holds it.** A fact about one argument sits above that argument, a fact about the block in its header, and a fact a consumer needs in a description or the README.

3. **Every claim is checkable.** A security or behaviour claim names the argument or address that enforces it. A reason is written only when the code, its history, a person or the vendor's documentation confirms it.

4. **Documenting changes no behaviour.** It touches comments, `description` strings, the order of arguments in variable and output blocks, READMEs and the documentation tooling, nothing else. A missing `type`, `sensitive` or `validation`, or a refactor, is a code change to propose separately. After a documentation-only change, `terraform plan` shows no changes.
Every block that manages, reads, moves or checks infrastructure carries a header: labelled sections in a comment directly above its first line.
# Purpose: Stores the audit records that the compliance exports read.
# Rationale: Kept apart from the application data bucket so that retention and access can
# Security: Public access is blocked by aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.audit_logs.
# Caution: Destroying this bucket fails while it holds objects, because force_destroy is
- **H1.** The header sits directly above the block's first line, with no blank line between them.
- **H2.** A section starts `# Label: ` with one of the five labels below, in the table's order, each at most once.
- **H3.** A section continues on lines that start with `#` and three spaces.

- **H4.** A section is one or more complete sentences ending in a full stop, at most three lines long; detail beyond that belongs in the README or an ADR that `See:` points to. `See:` holds references instead of sentences, one per line.
- **H5.** `Purpose:` starts with a present-tense verb (`Stores`, `Grants`, `Routes`, `Reads`, `Provisions`) and names the block's role in this system, never its resource type.
- **H6.** Comment lines are at most 100 characters long.
- **H7.** Scanner and linter directives (`#trivy:ignore:…`, `# tflint-ignore: …`) come last, directly above the block's first line.
- **H8.** Nothing else goes in a header: no blank `#` lines, no free text, no other labels.
| `Purpose:` | What the block is for, in this system | Always, except on a variable or an output |

| `Rationale:` | Why it is built this way rather than the obvious way | A competent maintainer reading only this block and the provider documentation would be tempted to change it: a non-default value, a workaround, a hard-coded value, a version held back, a data source where a resource would be expected, a deliberate exception to a convention |

| `Security:` | Which access, exposure, secret, encryption or audit control the block enforces, weakens or relies on, and where that is enforced | The block grants or denies access, exposes anything beyond its own network, creates, stores or passes a secret or key, configures encryption or audit logging, weakens any of these, or carries a scanner suppression |

| `Caution:` | What breaks or is lost when the block changes or goes, which a plan does not show | Replacement loses data, a change causes downtime or needs a manual step, something outside this configuration depends on it, a deletion safeguard is off, or an operation cannot be undone |
| `See:` | Where the longer story lives: an ADR's repository path, an upstream issue, a vendor page | The Rationale describes a workaround (link the upstream issue) or a decision an ADR records |
A `Security:` section that weakens a control says what compensates. One that justifies a suppression names the check.
| `provider` with `alias` | Required, and its Purpose says why a second configuration exists |
| `variable`, `output` | Optional, and never with `Purpose:`, because the `description` is the purpose |

Any comment directly above a top-level block is its header and follows the format. The only comments allowed outside a block are a licence notice at the top of a file (`Copyright` and `SPDX-License-Identifier` lines, then a blank line) and `tflint-ignore-file` directives.

A comment inside a block sits on its own lines directly above the argument or nested block it explains, at the same indentation, with no blank line between. Write plain sentences. The only labels inside a block are `Security:` and `Caution:`, so that `grep -rn '# Security:'` lists every security decision in the codebase. Never put a comment at the end of a line of code.
| A comment is required above | It says |
| `depends_on`, in any block | Why the implicit dependency is not enough |
| `prevent_destroy`, `create_before_destroy`, `ignore_changes`, `replace_triggered_by`, `action_trigger` | Why the rule exists; for `ignore_changes`, what changes the attribute outside Terraform |

| `count` or `for_each`, unless the expression is a reference, a null-safe one such as `coalesce(var.rules, [])`, `toset()` of either, or a toggle such as `var.enabled ? 1 : 0` or `var.rule != null ? [var.rule] : []` | What one instance is and what keys it |

| A literal that something outside the code dictates, such as a retention, timeout, size, threshold, CIDR range or port set by a policy, a measurement, a vendor limit or another system. A conventional value a maintainer can change knowing only the provider documentation, such as a DNS `ttl = 300`, needs none | Where the number comes from |
| A version constraint narrower or older than the rest of the codebase uses | Why, and what lifts it |
| A setting that weakens access or encryption: `0.0.0.0/0`, a `*` in IAM, public access, disabled encryption, logging or TLS verification | `Security:`, why it is acceptable and what compensates |
| A setting that removes a deletion safeguard: `force_destroy = true`, `deletion_protection = false`, `skip_final_snapshot = true` | `Caution:`, what is lost and why that is acceptable |
| A workaround for provider or API behaviour | What it works around, the upstream issue URL, and, when it is known, the condition for removing it |
| A suppression directive | Its justification, directly above it: a `Security:` sentence naming the check for a scanner, a reason for `tflint-ignore` |

When the fact concerns the whole block, it goes in the header instead. A `precondition`, `postcondition` or `check` assertion documents itself through its `error_message`: one complete sentence stating the requirement.
description = "Days an audit record is kept before it expires. Must be at least 400."
error_message = "retention_days must be at least 400, the audit lookback period in days."

- **V1.** Every variable has a `type` and a `description`. Arguments go in this order: `type`, `description`, `default`, `sensitive`, `nullable`, `ephemeral`, `const`, `deprecated`, then `validation` blocks.

- **V2.** The description is written for the caller: what the value is, its unit or format, any constraint the caller must meet, and what `null`, empty or the default means when that is not obvious. One or two sentences.
- **V3.** It opens with a noun phrase without an article (`Name of…`, `Number of…`, `ARN of…`). A `bool` opens with `Whether`: "Whether to block public access to the bucket."

- **V4.** It never restates the type, or the default as a bare value ("Defaults to 400"), because terraform-docs prints both; what the default means, and the constraints a caller must meet, are V2's to state. Nor does it say "This variable", name internal addresses, or carry maintainer notes. Those are comments: above the argument they concern, or in the header when they concern the whole variable.
- **V5.** An `object` type gets a heredoc description: the summary sentence, a blank line, then one bullet per attribute, ``- `name`: Sentence.``, saying what leaving out an optional attribute means.
- **V6.** A secret is `sensitive = true`, and its description says what the secret is for and where callers get it, never an example value.
- **V7.** A validation `error_message` is one complete sentence naming the variable and the values it accepts.
- **V8.** Deprecate with ``deprecated = "Use `new_name` instead."`` where `required_version` allows it, and otherwise open the description with ``Deprecated: use `new_name` instead.``
description = "ARN of the audit log bucket, for granting write access in log shippers' IAM policies."
- **O1.** Every output has a `description`. Arguments go in this order: `type`, `description`, `value`, `sensitive`, `ephemeral`, `deprecated`, `depends_on`, then `precondition` blocks.
- **O2.** The description says what the value is, its format, and when it is null or empty, adding what it is for when that is not obvious. V3's opening and V4's exclusions apply.
- **O3.** A map says what keys it. A list says its order, when the order means something.
- **O4.** A secret output is `sensitive = true`, and its description gives no hint of the value.
- **O5.** New outputs get a `type` once `required_version` excludes Terraform before 1.15.
- **L1.** Locals used by several files live in `locals.tf`; locals used by one file sit at the top of that file.
- **L2.** A local whose expression contains a `for` expression or a conditional gets a comment directly above it, saying what the value is and, for a collection, what its keys and elements are.
- **L3.** Any other local is named so that it needs no comment. Groups of locals are separated by a blank line, not by heading comments.

Every directory holding `.tf` files gets a `README.md`: root configurations, child modules and examples. Two kinds have none: a nested module of a published module repository that is internal on purpose, because the standard module structure reads a missing README as internal, and a helper module under `tests/`. Hand-written sections come first, in a fixed order, and terraform-docs generates the reference between `<!-- BEGIN_TF_DOCS -->` and `<!-- END_TF_DOCS -->`, which ends the file and is never edited by hand.

Read `references/readme.md` before creating or changing a README or the documentation tooling. Its section order wins over general document-type advice from writing-documentation, which still applies inside each section.
- The block type, name, argument or value in words: "Creates an S3 bucket", "Sets the timeout".
- A paraphrase of the provider documentation.
- History: who changed what, when, or from what. Git holds it.
- An internal ticket number in place of the reason. Write the reason; the commit and the pull request carry the link. An upstream issue URL in `See:` is fine.
- Banners, dividers or section headings. Split the file instead, named after the group, such as `network.tf`.
- `//` or `/* */` comments, including a `/** */` header for terraform-docs to extract. Module prose lives in the README.
- `TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK` or `XXX`. Open work goes in the tracker, and a known limitation in a `Caution:` or the README.
- Owners, teams or contacts. CODEOWNERS and tags hold them.
- Figures that drift: costs, counts, current sizes. State the invariant behind them instead, such as "billed per provisioned hour".
- Plain, present tense, complete sentences. No em dashes, no filler.

- In `#` comments, write addresses and names bare, as Terraform prints them: `aws_s3_bucket.audit_logs`, `module.network`, `var.retention_days`. In descriptions and READMEs, which render as Markdown, wrap identifiers and literal values in backticks.
- Spell as the repository already does.
## Where the rules underdetermine the answer

**An obvious resource still gets a Purpose, about its role.** `aws_s3_bucket_versioning` becomes "Keeps earlier versions of audit records so that an overwrite can be undone", not "Enables versioning".
**Rationale looks back, Caution looks forward.** Why it was built this way is Rationale; what happens to whoever changes it is Caution.

**Security is access, exposure, secrets, encryption and audit; Caution is loss.** A disabled deletion safeguard is a Caution. When a Rationale's reason is security, write it as Security, because finding it by `grep` matters more.
**Twenty similar blocks get twenty Purposes.** If they genuinely share one, that argues for `for_each`, which is a code change to propose rather than make.

**An unknown reason is never guessed.** Look first: `git log -S '<value>' -- <file>`, `git blame`, the pull request, the ADRs, the README, the provider documentation. Then ask. Unattended, write only what is verifiable, leave the section or comment out, and list the open question in your summary. Never write a placeholder. A literal you cannot place, not knowing whether something outside the code dictates it, is such an open question.

**A workaround's link sits with the workaround.** One confined to an argument carries its upstream issue URL in the comment above that argument. `See:` is for a workaround or decision that the header's Rationale describes.

**Version-gated arguments follow `required_version`.** Output `type` and `deprecated` on variables and outputs need Terraform 1.15 or later, and ephemeral variables and outputs need 1.10. Use them only when `required_version` excludes older releases. For OpenTofu, check its own documentation instead.

A documentation convention the repository already writes down and follows wins over this skill. Name the difference, follow the convention, get as close to this skill as it allows, and ask before breaking it. A linter or CI check that actually runs beats prose.

On an incidental change, bring the blocks you add or change up to this standard and report violations elsewhere rather than fixing them unasked. When documenting a module is the task, the whole module meets it.
1. Read before writing: `required_version`, the README, `.terraform-docs.yml`, `.tflint.hcl`, and any CONTRIBUTING or style guide.
2. Gather the reasons the code does not show, from history and people, before writing any Rationale, Security or Caution.

3. Write headers, in-block comments, descriptions and locals comments. `references/block-catalogue.md` has a worked example for every block kind and the common failures as before-and-after pairs; read it before documenting a kind you have not done in this session, or when a call is not obvious.
4. Update the README and regenerate its reference.
5. Validate, then report what you documented, the open questions, the violations you left alone, and the code changes you propose.

These are unattended invocations, for agents and CI. Something written for people shows what a person types instead. Run the tools the project has, and when one is missing, say which check did not run instead of installing or building it unasked. Without terraform-docs, leave the README's markers in place, empty or as they were, for the next run to fill.
tflint --recursive                            # where .tflint.hcl enables the documentation rules

The checker exits 0 when clean, 1 with findings, printed as `path:line: rule: message`, and 2 on a usage error. It decides every rule a script can: header presence, format, labels and order, directive placement and justification, the comments required on `depends_on`, lifecycle rules, `count`, `for_each` and locals, comment syntax and placement, the argument order and description shape of variables and outputs, and README presence and structure. `--internal` names nested modules, by path or glob, that have no README on purpose.

It cannot tell whether a comment is true, whether a Rationale or Caution is owed, or whether a description says what a consumer needs. The checklist below covers that, and a passing checker does not excuse it.
- Every Purpose names a role, not a resource type, and makes sense to someone who has never seen the system.
- Every Rationale, Security and Caution was confirmed in the code or a source, and every Security claim names what enforces it.
- No comment restates code, carries history or a ticket number, or sits at the end of a line.
- Every variable and output description says what the value is, its unit or format, and what null or empty means where it matters, in the caller's terms.
- The README's sections are in order, its reference is regenerated, and nothing between the markers was edited by hand.
- The checker passes on what you changed, and the change would leave `terraform plan` empty.

Read on 2026-10-26: HashiCorp's Terraform style guide (`developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/style`), which sets the base variable and output argument orders that V1 and O1 extend with the newer arguments; the standard module structure; the `variable` and `output` block references, which ask for descriptions written for the module's consumer; the Terraform 1.15 release notes for output `type` and `deprecated`; the terraform-docs 0.24.0 configuration reference; the TFLint Terraform ruleset and annotations; and the inline suppression syntax of Checkov and Trivy. The header labels, the comment criteria and the README sections are this skill's own, not HashiCorp's.

Every directory holding `.tf` files is a module and has a `README.md`: each root configuration, each child module under `modules/`, and each example under `examples/`.

Two kinds of directory have none. A nested module of a published module repository that is internal on purpose, because HashiCorp's standard module structure treats a nested module without a README as internal; name it to the checker with `--internal`. And helper modules under `tests/`, which the checker skips.
A repository root with no `.tf` files of its own is a landing page rather than a module, and the writing-repository-readmes skill covers it.
The sections come in this order. A section is present exactly when its condition holds: never empty, never "None" or "N/A".
| 1 | `# <name>` | Always | The directory name, or the repository name at the root of a module repository |
| 2 | Summary, no heading | Always | One to three sentences. The first stands alone and opens with a present-tense verb: what the module provisions, and for what |
| 3 | `## Usage` | Always | A child module: a `module` block. A root configuration or an example: the commands a person types |
| 4 | `## Architecture` | Callers must know how the parts connect to use the module correctly | Prose and a diagram, never a restated resource list |
| 5 | `## Prerequisites` | Something must exist or be done first; always for a root configuration | A list: what must exist, and who creates it |
| 6 | `## Security` | Any block in the module has a `Security:` header section | What the module exposes or grants, what it encrypts and with which key, and what remains the caller's job |

| 7 | `## Operations` | Any block has a `Caution:` header section; always for a root configuration | Where state lives, which configurations this one reads and is read by, manual steps, and inputs whose change replaces resources |
| 8 | Generated reference | Always | terraform-docs output between the markers, ending the file |

An example has sections 1, 2, 3 and 8 only. No other heading appears at level 2: licence and contribution notes live in `LICENSE` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`, upgrade steps under Operations, and the inputs, outputs and resources in the generated reference. Level-3 headings inside a section are free.

- **R1.** The `module` block in Usage sets `source` as callers write it: a registry address with `version`, a Git URL with `?ref=` and a tag, or, for a local module, the relative path from the configuration that calls it. It sets the required inputs only. When the current version cannot be found, leave `version` out and report it; never write a placeholder such as `<version>`.

- **R2.** Example values are reserved for documentation: the account ID `123456789012`, the address ranges `192.0.2.0/24`, `198.51.100.0/24` and `203.0.113.0/24`, and domains under `example.com`. Never a real account, address, domain or secret.
- **R3.** Commands are what a person types. No `-auto-approve`, `-input=false` or `-no-color`, which are for automation.
- **R4.** Usage ends with a link to `examples/` when the directory exists.

- **R5.** Links to files in the repository are relative, except in a module published to a registry, where they are commit-specific absolute URLs, as the standard module structure asks, so that a released version keeps pointing at its own files.
- **R6.** A diagram is Mermaid where the README is read on GitHub or GitLab, and an image otherwise.

- **R7.** Security and Operations restate for consumers what the headers record for maintainers, in consumer terms, with input names rather than resource addresses. That is the one sanctioned overlap between the two.
- **R8.** The register is SKILL.md's: plain, present tense, identifiers and literal values in backticks.

- Public access is blocked on the bucket, and no input turns it off.
- Objects are encrypted with the key passed as `kms_key_arn`; its key policy is the caller's to write.
- `log_shipper_policy_json` grants write access to the `logs/` prefix and nothing else.
- Changing `bucket_name` replaces the bucket. Objects are not copied, and the old bucket cannot be destroyed while it holds any.

terraform-docs writes the Requirements, Providers, Modules, Resources, Inputs and Outputs tables between the markers, from the code and its `description` strings. That is why a description is written for the consumer: it is the consumer's documentation. Nothing between the markers is edited by hand, and nothing follows the end marker.
Regenerate it in the same change as the code it documents. A README whose reference is stale fails `terraform-docs --output-check`.
One file at the repository root serves every module, because terraform-docs falls back to the configuration in the directory it runs from when the module directory has none.
Each setting that departs from the default is a decision:
- `sections.hide` drops the header and footer, so that module prose has one home, the README above the markers, and a stray `/** */` comment in `main.tf` cannot reach it.
- `sort.by: required` lists the inputs a caller must set first.
- `hide-empty` leaves out empty tables, rather than printing "No outputs."

- `lockfile: false` documents the version constraints from the code rather than the versions a lock file pinned, so the tables do not change on every provider upgrade, and a child module without a committed lock file renders the same everywhere.

- `read-comments: false` keeps maintainer comments out of the consumer's tables. A variable without a `description` shows an empty cell, where TFLint and the checker catch it, rather than borrowing the comment above it.
- `indent: 2` puts the generated headings at level 2, beside the hand-written sections.

- `version` is the oldest release with every setting used here. Pin the exact terraform-docs and TFLint versions in the project's toolchain file as well, so that every machine generates identical tables.

description: Writes and revises talks in a deck made from the slides template (slides.mdx), turning a topic, outline, article or README into a narrative of one-idea slides with sentence headlines, visual evidence instead of bullet lists, builds for sequences, code that fits the frame and steps through with highlights, diffs and magic moves, and speaker notes that carry the detail, then checks every slide with pnpm check before finishing. Use when asked to write, outline, restructure, shorten, review, fix or brand a talk, presentation, deck or slides.mdx, including requests such as "add a slide about X", "turn this post into a 20-minute talk" or "the code on slide 7 does not fit". Not for .pptx, Keynote, Slidev or Marp decks. Load mermaid-diagrams alongside it for diagram syntax, and hand the prose of speaker notes to humanizer.

**A slide is what the audience reads while the speaker talks; everything else goes in `<Notes>`.** Most bad decks are the speaker's script projected on a wall, and every rule below follows from not doing that.

**Check that the deck comes from the slides template.** `slides.mdx` at the root with `plugins/remark-slides.ts` next to it says so. Without them the syntax here does not apply: say which kind of deck it is and apply only the design rules. The deck's own syntax is documented in its `README.md`, which wins where it and this skill disagree.
## Start from the talk, not the slides
Before writing a slide, settle four things, from the request and the material, and state any you had to assume:
- **The audience**, and what they already know.
- **The length.** Budget about one content slide per minute, and plan for 80% of the slot.
- **The big idea**, one sentence with a verb and a stake: what the audience should remember if they remember nothing else. Every slide supports it, and material that does not is cut.
- **The arc**: the problem and the promise in the first two or three slides, the argument, and a last slide that restates the big idea.

The deck a project starts with includes a tour of the template from `chapters/tour.mdx`: a real talk replaces that `<Include>` in `slides.mdx` with its own slides, and deletes `chapters/tour.mdx`, `chapters/example.mdx` and `snippets/counter.ts` once nothing uses them. Never write the talk into the tour's files: `weft update` changes them.

Then **write every headline first, in order, and read them as a paragraph.** If they do not make the argument on their own, no slide body will fix it. No agenda before the problem is stated, and no "Questions?" or "Thank you" as the last slide; the takeaway stays up during questions. `references/talk-structure.md` has the arc, signposting and timing in detail: read it when outlining a new talk or restructuring one.

Every content slide's `##` is a full sentence stating what the slide shows, in at most two lines: about 90 characters at `##`, 70 at `#`. A topic label makes the audience work out the point; a sentence tells them, and they remember it (79% against 69% correct in Alley's study). A question headline does worse still, unless a later step answers it.
## Caching cut p99 latency from 800 ms to 120 ms        ← the claim
`<Cover>`, `<Section>`, `<Statement>` and `<Quote>` are exempt: their content is the headline. Never put a sentence headline inside a `<Columns>` cell, where 22 characters fit on a line.

The body shows why the headline is true: code, a diagram, an image, a table, one number as a `<Stat value label>`, or two things side by side in `<Columns>`. Not a list of the things you will say. When a sentence has to sit beside the code or the image it is about, give the evidence the wider column and centre both: `<Columns widths="3:2" align="center">`.
- **About 20 visible words on a content slide**, counting the headline and body text but not code or notes. At 33 or more the audience reads instead of listening.
- **A list has at most four items**, each at most two lines, and never stands alone under a headline.
- **The sentences you will say go in `<Notes>`**, as cues, not a script: the audience cannot read and listen at once.
- **Compare on one slide**, never across two: `<Columns>`, a `diff`, a magic move.
- **Label the thing itself.** No legend, no "see left", no "as shown below".
Before, the speaker's script on the canvas:
- We retry failed requests up to 5 times
- Retries use exponential backoff starting at 100 ms
- Without jitter, clients retry at the same moment
- This caused the outage on 12 March
- Adding full jitter spreads retries out
- p99 recovery time dropped from 14 min to 90 s
After, the claim, the change as evidence, and the detail in notes:
## Full jitter cut outage recovery from 14 minutes to 90 seconds
- 12 March: every client retried in lockstep and the database never recovered
- Source for 14 min to 90 s: the incident review
Every number, date, version and quotation on a slide comes from the user's material, with its source in that slide's notes. Never invent a figure to make a slide land.

`<Steps>` reveals a list item by item and `<Step>` reveals one block; highlight steps and magic moves build code. **Build a graphic or code as you talk about its parts; do not drip-feed text bullets** unless the last one is a punch line. Keep a text build to four items.

The print view and the overview show every slide fully revealed, so **the last step of a slide must make sense on its own**: a highlight sequence ends on `all`, which also leaves folds shut, and a magic move's last version is the one worth printing.
Read `references/code-slides.md` before writing or editing any slide with code: the fence options, the measured limits and the patterns for showing change. The rules that decide most code slides:
- **One idea per code slide, and the `##` says what the code does or proves.**

- **It fits at full size.** At 15 px a line holds 88 characters across the slide, 39 in a `<Columns>` cell, and 48 in the wide cell of `widths="3:2"` (84, 35 and 43 with `lineNumbers`). A block under a one-line headline holds 13 lines, 11 with `title=`; under a two-line headline, 12 and 10. Code that does not fit is shrunk to fit, down to 80%, and `pnpm check` warns about it: **treat that warning as a failure** and cut, split or add `maxLines`.

- **Cut what is not the point**, imports, boilerplate and error handling included, and mark the gap with `// …`. Say in the notes when shown code would not compile as is. Where the code must stay whole, fold instead: `fold={4-11}` hides those lines behind one line until a step highlights inside them.
- **Show change as change**: a `diff`, `diff split` or a magic move, never two full listings.
- **Prefer real code**: `file="./snippets/…"` reads it from a file that `pnpm typecheck` compiles.

A `mermaid` fence in the deck becomes an SVG when it builds, so load `mermaid-diagrams` for the syntax and its readability rules. Its rule against diagrams in files of their own is written for GitHub; here the fence goes in `slides.mdx` like any other. On a 16:9 slide keep to about six nodes, prefer `flowchart LR`, and keep labels to a word or two: the build warns when a diagram is too wide, and the check warns when its labels end up under 18 px.
The canvas is 960 × 540 and scales to the screen, so a canvas pixel is a point on a standard PowerPoint slide, and accessibility guidance applies directly.
- **Nothing the audience must read is under 18 px, except code at 15 px.** Body text is 20 px, tables and callouts 18 px. No `text-sm` or `text-xs` on content, and no `class="text-sm"` on a fence.
- **Contrast**: no `text-muted-foreground/70` or lighter on content, and nothing important only in a code comment, which is 3.9:1 in the dark theme.
- **Colour never carries meaning alone**: the deck is shown in light and dark, and printed.
- **Never hide overflow.** No `overflow-hidden`, `max-h-*`, `scale-*`, `zoom` or smaller text added to make a slide pass. Split the slide.
Read `references/brand.md` when a deck must follow a brand or a logo: where the colours, fonts and logo go, and how much of them a slide can carry.
`slides.mdx` is MDX, not Markdown, and one mistake can blank the whole deck:
- A literal `{` or `}` in prose is JavaScript: write `\{`, or put it in inline code. A bare `{word}` compiles, then throws in the browser.

- Comments are `{/* … */}`, never ``. A `<` before a digit breaks the parse: write "under 100 ms". `
` must be `
`, and links are `[text](url)`, never ``.
- Markdown inside a component needs blank lines around it, or it stays one inline line.

- `---` needs a blank line above it. Right under a line of text it underlines that line into a `##` heading, and the slide or the `<Columns>` does not split; the build warns `"---" right under "…" makes it a heading`.
These commands are for you; none of them belong in a slide or its notes.

1. **Run `pnpm check`.** It type-checks the slides (a wrong prop or a misspelt component is an error), builds, renders every step of every slide, fails on content that runs off a slide or out of a code frame at any step, warns about code or a diagram shrunk to fit, and writes an image of every slide to `.tmp/export/`. Fix every failure and every warning.

2. **Look at every image in `.tmp/export/` as the audience would.** Read the headlines in order first, then each slide against the rules above. A passing check is not a good talk. An author reviewing their own slides explains the problems away, so hand this to a fresh context where you can: a subagent given the images, the headlines in order and the checklist below, asked to list the problems on each slide. It judges; measuring sizes and overflow is the check's job. Where no subagent can run, or one does not report, review in two passes yourself: write down every problem on every slide first, then fix them.
3. **Fix, rerun, and stop after a clean pass.**
`references/failure-modes.md` lists each failure with a test that finds it and the fix: read it when reviewing a deck, or when the check or the look finds something you cannot place.
1. **The audience can read it** beats fitting the content on one slide: split the slide, never shrink the text.
2. **One idea per slide** beats the slide count: cut an idea from the talk before packing two onto a slide.
3. **The user's explicit instruction** beats the style rules here, but not legibility or the check; say what you kept against the guidance and why it matters.
4. **The fully revealed slide makes sense** beats a clever build.
- The big idea is one sentence, and the headlines read in order make the argument.
- Every content slide's `##` is a sentence of at most two lines.
- No content slide is a headline and a list, and no list has more than four items.
- Every content slide has `<Notes>`, and no sentence of the notes is on the slide.
- Every figure on a slide comes from the user's material, with its source in the notes.
- Code fits at full size, ends its highlights on `all`, and shows change as change.
- Nothing the audience must read is under 18 px, or 15 px for code.
- `pnpm check` passed with no warnings, and every image in `.tmp/export/` was looked at.
- The last slide is the takeaway, not "Questions?".
- The prose in the notes went through `humanizer`.
Read 2026-09-28; check them before relying on a number, since guidance moves.

- Garner and Alley, "How the design of presentation slides affects audience comprehension", *International Journal of Engineering Education* 29(6), 2013: sentence headlines with visual evidence against topic headlines with bullets, 21 against 42 words a slide.
- Alley, Schreiber, Ramsdell and Muffo, "How the design of headlines in presentation slides affects audience retention", *Technical Communication* 53(2), 2006.
- Alley and Neeley, "Rethinking the design of presentation slides", *Technical Communication* 52(4), 2005.

- Mayer and Fiorella, "Principles for reducing extraneous processing in multimedia learning", *Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning*, 2014: coherence, redundancy, spatial and temporal contiguity.
- Kosslyn, Kievit, Russell and Shephard, "PowerPoint presentation flaws and failures", *Frontiers in Psychology* 3:230, 2012.
- Microsoft, "Make your PowerPoint presentations accessible", and W3C, WCAG 2.2 success criteria 1.4.3 and 1.4.11: 18 pt, 4.5:1 and 3:1.
- Simon Peyton Jones, "How to give a great research talk"; Nancy Duarte, *Resonate* and *Slidedocs*; Patrick Winston, "How to Speak", MIT OpenCourseWare.

"notes": "A content slide whose headline is a topic label, or longer than two lines, fails. A content slide that is only a headline and a list, or any list of more than four items, fails. Putting the speaker's sentences on the canvas instead of in <Notes> fails. Shrinking text below 18 px or code below 15 px, or hiding overflow with overflow-hidden, max-h, scale or zoom, fails; the fix is to cut or split. Finishing without running pnpm check, with an overflow or a shrink warning left, or without looking at the rendered slides fails. Inventing a number, a date or a quotation fails. Rewriting a deck that already follows the rules fails. Applying this template's syntax to a deck made with something else fails. Answering a request that belongs to another skill fails. Putting the logo on every slide, redrawing a logo the brand publishes, or choosing a text colour on the brand colour without computing its contrast fails.",

# A deck in a brand's colours

Where a brand goes in this deck, and how much of it a slide can carry. A brand is there to be recognised, not to fill the slides: the audience should know whose talk it is from the first slide and then look at the evidence.

- **Colours** are the tokens in `src/index.css`, once in `:root` and once in `.dark`: `--primary` is the brand colour and `--primary-foreground` the text on it; `--foreground` and `--muted-foreground` take the brand's text greys, if it has them; `--ring` and `--chart-1` to `--chart-5` usually follow the primary. The code highlight, `<Stat>` numbers and the cover's glow take the primary; diagrams take the text colours and the chart tokens.
- **Full slides in the brand colour** are `<Cover variant="primary">`, and the same on `<Section>`, `<Statement>` and `<Quote>`. Never rebuild them with colour classes by hand.

- **Fonts** come from an `@fontsource` package imported in `src/index.css`, with `--font-sans` or `--font-heading` pointing at it. Keep the deck's font when the brand's is not licensed for the web; a close free face beats a missing one.
- **Logo files** go in `public/`, referenced without a leading slash, such as `logo.svg`.
**Use the brand's own files**, from its brand guide, press kit or website, never a redrawing. When only a bitmap exists, trace it to SVG and compare the two side by side at the size they will show.

**Show it on the cover and the last slide, not on every slide.** A logo in the corner of every slide is decoration the audience stops seeing, and it takes room from the evidence (Mayer and Fiorella's coherence principle). Keep the clear space the brand asks for, and never stretch, recolour or add an effect the brand does not use itself.

**The brand colour marks what matters, sparingly**: the cover, section slides, the number on a `<Stat>`, the highlight in code. Emphasis works when there is little of it (Mayer and Fiorella's signalling principle). Body text stays in the foreground colour, and no fact exists only in colour.
A slide filled with the brand colour is a landmark. Use one for the cover, each section and the closing slide, and keep content slides on the background, where evidence reads best.

**Compute it, never eyeball it.** WCAG 2.2 asks for 4.5:1 for text, and 3:1 for text of 24 px and larger or 18.7 px bold, in both themes. White on a saturated red or orange is often only just above 4.5:1, so text on the brand colour stays large, and secondary text on it at 90% white or more. A brand colour used as text on white needs the same 4.5:1.
Either design the dark theme too, or pin the deck to one theme with `colorScheme` in the frontmatter.
These commands are for you, not for the slides.
1. `pnpm check`, then look at the cover, a section slide and a content slide at full size in `.tmp/export/`.
2. If the deck can switch to dark (<kbd>D</kbd>), `node scripts/export.ts --check --theme dark` after the build, and look again.
3. Put the cover next to the brand's own logo and compare: colour, shape, and the space around the mark.

The fence options of this deck, the space a slide has for code, and the patterns for the things a talk does with code. The deck's `README.md` has the same option table and wins where the two differ; a change to `plugins/remark-code.ts` updates both.
Written after the language, in any order:
| `title="src/app.ts"` | Title bar with the file name and a copy button; costs about two lines of height |
| `lineNumbers`, `startLine=10` | Line numbers, from 10; cost four columns |
| `{2,4-6}` | Highlights those lines and dims the rest |
| `file="./snippets/app.ts"` | The code of a real file; `#L10-24` for lines, `#name` for a `// #region name` |
| `maxLines=10` | At most that many lines, scrolled to what is highlighted |
| `fold={4-11}`, `fold=#name` | Those lines, or a region of a `file=` snippet, behind one line until a step highlights inside them or a click opens them |
| `diff` | `+` and `-` lines shown as added and removed; `git diff` output works as is |
| `diff split` | The same, starting before and after side by side |
| `diff magic-move` | The diff played from before to after in one step |
| `class="mx-auto w-fit"` | Classes on the frame, never a smaller text size |

A four-backtick `md magic-move` fence holds several fences, one per version. `<CodeTabs>` around several fences makes tabs. Shiki's notation comments mark a line and disappear from the slide: `// [!code ++]`, `// [!code --]`, `// [!code highlight]`, `// [!code focus]`, `// [!code error]`, `// [!code warning]`, `// [!code word:name]`.

Text above or below the block takes from the same budget. Past these limits the code shrinks to fit, down to 80%, and `pnpm check` warns: shrunk code is under the size a room can read, so treat the warning as a failure. Aim well inside the limits; eight lines and 60 columns read comfortably. Code beside the sentence it proves goes in the wide cell of `<Columns widths="3:2" align="center">`, which centres the sentence level with the code; a narrow cell holds a short config or a list, not a function.
Highlight steps are the idiom for "look here, now here": one step per sentence you will say, ending on `all` because the print view shows the last step.
